Need to search first.# Notes on 1 Chronicles 1:28–54

**How these were gathered:** My tool allowance ran out partway through, so I couldn't open any page in full. Every note below comes from the long excerpts the search tool returned for each page. Some of those excerpts were cut short, and I've marked where that matters. The searches turned up nothing from Catholic or Orthodox sites (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org), from bibleodyssey.org, or about prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this passage. Those sections are left out.

---

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**Overview (vv. 28–54)**
- Chronicles narrows the list here. Every nation except Abraham's family has now been dropped. Henry adds that this doesn't mean no one outside Abraham's line found favour with God. He also urges readers to think about how many generations have come and gone, and how short our own time is. (Matthew Henry, Presbyterian) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/1-28.htm
- The order is deliberate. Abraham's other children (vv. 28–33) and Isaac's other son (vv. 34–54) come first, and then the book turns to Israel. (Bridgeway) https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/1-28.html
- Gill says the passage matches Genesis 25 (Abraham's sons) and Genesis 36 (Esau's line, and the kings and chiefs of Edom). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/1.htm
- The chapter ends with four short lists: Esau's sons, the founding fathers of Edom, Edom's kings, and the tribes that made up Edom. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/1-chronicles/

**v. 28**
- Isaac is named first even though he was younger, because he was the rightful heir. Sarah alone was Abraham's true wife. (Barnes) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/1-28.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary notes three things:
  - Abraham's new name is used straight away.
  - Naming these two sons apart from the others follows Genesis 21:12–13: Isaac carries the promise, and Ishmael will still become a nation.
  - Isaac is named first because he matters more, but Ishmael's line is dealt with first.
  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/1-28.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: Isaac comes first as "the son of the promise." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/1-28.htm
- Guzik: Isaac is the son of promise and covenant (Genesis 17–27). Ishmael was blessed as Abraham's son but did not inherit the covenant (Genesis 16, 21). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide_1Ch/1Ch_1.cfm
- Ishmael was about 14 years older but is listed second because Isaac was chosen to carry the line. (Zerr) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/1-chronicles-1.html
- Gaebelein also notes that the two are not in birth order. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/1-chronicles-1.html

**vv. 29–31**
- These twelve sons begin to fulfil God's promise to make Ishmael a great nation (Genesis 21:18). Guzik says that promise was ultimately fulfilled in the Arab peoples. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide_1Ch/1Ch_1.cfm
- Henry gives little space to the Ishmaelites. They were the bondwoman's children, not heirs with the child of promise. Following Galatians 4:22, he says they picture the unbelieving Jews who were rejected. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_001.cfm
- The Restoration Commentary says Ishmael's twelve sons were princes and founders of today's Arab nations. It describes his blessings as earthly rather than spiritual. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/1-chronicles-1.html

**v. 32**
- Clarke (Methodist) says "concubine" (Hebrew *pilegesh*) means a wife of the second rank, not a concubine in the modern sense. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/1-32.html
- Barnes says this verse and Genesis 25:6 show Keturah was a secondary wife, not a full wife. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/1-32.html
- GotQuestions points out that Genesis 25:1 calls her a "wife" while this verse calls her a "concubine." It offers two explanations: she could be called a wife of lower rank than Sarah, or she began as a concubine and was raised to wife after Sarah died. https://www.gotquestions.org/Keturah-in-the-Bible.html
- Guzik calls her Abraham's second wife, taken after Sarah's death. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide_1Ch/1Ch_1.cfm

**v. 33**
- Henry: Keturah's descendants, the Midianites, were "children of the east" and were sent away from Isaac (Genesis 25:6), so they are only named. He suggests Job was probably one of them, and that Midian became the leading branch, much as Judah did among the Jews. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/1-28.html

**v. 34**
- Of Isaac's two sons, only Israel was chosen as heir of the covenant. Esau's sons still mattered to God and had a place in His plan. (Guzik) https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide_1Ch/1Ch_1.cfm
- Esau was the firstborn but lost the blessing because he did not value his birthright. He became the founder of Edom. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/1-chronicles-1.html
- Gaebelein: Esau's line is given before Israel's, which follows in chapter 2. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/1-chronicles-1.html

**v. 35**
- Ryrie: Esau's descendants get a brief mention, but the writer's real interest is in Jacob's line. Esau is Edom. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-1-commentary
- Believer's Study Bible: the line not chosen is usually listed before the chosen line. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-1-commentary
- Although Esau did not inherit the covenant, God still kept His word to make him a nation (Genesis 25:23; 36:1). Eliphaz's line became the most prominent. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-1-commentary
- The Restoration Commentary gives name meanings: Eliphaz, "God is fine gold"; Reuel, "friend of God." It says Jeush, Jalam and Korah were sons of Oholibamah. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/1-chronicles-1.html
- TGC: Esau also married a daughter of Ishmael (Genesis 28:6–9), which joined the two lines. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/1-chronicles/

**v. 36**
- Gill: Timna was not a son. She was Eliphaz's concubine and Amalek's mother (Genesis 36:12), and the Arabic version reads the verse that way. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/1.htm
- NET Bible note: the Hebrew says simply "and Timna and Amalek." Genesis 36:12 shows Timna was the mother. Many manuscripts read "Zepho" for "Zephi." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=1Ch&chapter=1
- Keil & Delitzsch reject another scholar's (Bertheau's) "arbitrary" move of counting Timna as Esau's grandchild. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/1-38.htm
- Amalek's descendants became one of Israel's most persistent enemies. Kenaz is linked with the Kenizzites. https://biblehub.com/1_chronicles/1-36.htm
- Zerr suggests marking Esau, Eliphaz and Amalek, because the Amalekites were a well-known people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/1-chronicles-1.html

**v. 37**
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown links Reuel and Shammah with later Arab tribes. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/1-43.htm

**v. 38**
- Gill: Seir's family was not descended from Esau. They are listed because Esau and one of his sons married into them, and Esau's people took over their land. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/1-38.htm
- Poole: Seir was a prince of the Horites. Those of his people who did not merge with Esau's line were destroyed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/1-38.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: after Esau's people arrived, Mount Seir held twenty tribes. Thirteen were Edomite and seven were Seirite. The Seirites were the original inhabitants of the land. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/1-38.htm

**v. 39**
- NET note: this is perhaps the same Timna as in v. 36. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=1Ch&chapter=1

**vv. 40–42**
- The names match Genesis 36:20–27 apart from small spelling differences (for example Homam/Hemam, Alian/Alvan, Amram/Hemdan, Jakan/Akan). (Preacher's Homiletical) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/1-chronicles-1.html
- Gill: same as Genesis 36:20, with small differences in names. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/1.htm
- Guzik's study guide quotes a writer suggesting that Uz gave his name to Job's homeland, so Job may have been an early Edomite. The excerpt didn't show which verse this comment belongs to. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-1Ch/1Ch-1.cfm

**v. 43**
- Edom's kings came before Israel's. Guzik says God's timing has its own wisdom, sometimes clear to us and sometimes not. The list also shows that Esau was truly blessed even though he did not inherit the covenant. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-1/
- Ellicott (Anglican) compares Moses' request to Edom's king for passage (Numbers 20:14–21). He says Edom was the older people, settled earlier, so it was naturally ahead of Israel politically. He calls the note fitting in an introduction to David's royal house. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/1-43.htm
- Ellicott on names: "Bela son of Beor" is strikingly like "Balaam son of Beor," and Balaam may have been of royal birth. He takes "Dinhabah" to mean the place where the king gave judgment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/1-43.htm
- Geneva Bible note: the list shows God keeping His promise that kings would come from Esau. Eight kings ruled until David conquered Edom. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/1-43.htm
- Another note excerpted on the same page (its author isn't named) adds that Edom stayed important long after the Chronicler's time, and that the Herods were of Edomite descent. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/1-43.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: the passage repeats Genesis 36:31–39 word for word, apart from small omissions. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/1-43.htm
- Precept Austin: this marks the turn from Esau's family to Edom's rulers. Edom had an organised monarchy long before Israel did. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-1-commentary
- Trapp: kings were crowned but chiefs ("dukes") were not. Israel had judges, then kings, then governors after the exile, and Edom followed a similar pattern. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/1-chronicles-1.html

**v. 44**
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown mentions the view that Jobab was Job. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/1-43.htm
- Bozrah was one of Edom's main cities. The prophets later use it to stand for Edom itself (Isaiah 34:6; Jeremiah 49:13). https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-1-commentary

**vv. 44–50 (the pattern of succession)**
- Keil & Delitzsch: no son ever follows his father, and each king comes from a different family and place. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/36-35.html
- Henry, citing Bishop Patrick: the kings seem to have been chosen by election, not by descent. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/36-35.html
- Precept Austin: the lack of a dynasty may point to a tribal or confederated system. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-1-commentary
- TGC: the title seems to have been earned by strong leaders through notable deeds. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/1-chronicles/

**v. 50**
- Keil & Delitzsch on differences from Genesis 36:
  - Genesis has "Hadar" where Chronicles has "Hadad." They put this down to a copyist's error.
  - "Pai/Pau" is a different pronunciation of the same name.
  - Chronicles leaves out "son of Achbor."
  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/1-43.htm

**v. 51a ("Then Hadad died")**
- Keil & Delitzsch: Genesis doesn't record this king's death because he was still alive in Moses' day. Chronicles adds it because he had long been dead by then. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/1-43.htm
- Iain Duguid notes that the Chronicler adds "Hadad died" and names no successor. The excerpt cuts off before his conclusion. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-1-commentary

**vv. 51b–54**
- Keil & Delitzsch: "and the chiefs of Edom were…" could mean chiefs replaced the kings. They think it more likely the phrase just links ideas, or means chiefs ruled alongside the kings. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/1-43.htm
- Ellicott: these verses copy Genesis 36:31–43 with only ordinary copying differences. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-1.html

---

## 2. Where Protestant teachers differ

I found no clear split along denominational lines. What I did find were differences between individual teachers:

**v. 43: Why Edom had kings first, and how that relates to Israel's kings**
- **Matthew Henry (Presbyterian):** "before any king" means before Moses' time, since Moses was "king in Jeshurun" (Deuteronomy 33:5). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/36-35.html
- **Coffman (Church of Christ, on the Genesis parallel):** the phrase looks ahead to God's promise of kings from Jacob (Genesis 35:11). It does not show the text was written after Saul. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/36-35.html
- **J. Vernon McGee (independent dispensationalist, on Genesis 36):** Israel got the idea of kings from neighbours like Edom. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/36-35.html
- **A BibleHub Q&A article** says the opposite: Israel's monarchy was not copied from Edom but was a separate institution set up by God. It also sees a deliberate eight-and-eight pattern of kings and chiefs as a sign of divine authorship. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_are_Edomite_kings_significant.htm

**vv. 29–31 and 43: How Ishmael and Edom are interpreted spiritually**
- **Henry** reads Ishmael through Galatians 4 as a picture of the unbelieving Jews. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_001.cfm
- **The Restoration Commentary** says the kings and chiefs are listed to show where opposition to Israel comes from: a lasting war between "flesh" and "spirit." It calls the Edomite chiefs Arabs descended from Ishmael, which conflicts with the text and with Gill and Poole, who say Esau and the Horite Seirites. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/1-chronicles-1.html
- **Guzik (Calvary Chapel, under the Pentecostal/charismatic heading in your list)** is more positive: Esau was "a blessed man" and had a place in God's plan. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-1/

**v. 32: What "concubine" means for Keturah**
- **Clarke (Methodist):** a second-rank wife, not a concubine in our sense. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/1-32.html
- **Barnes (Presbyterian):** not a full wife. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/1-32.html
- **GotQuestions:** offers ways to reconcile the two. https://www.gotquestions.org/Keturah-in-the-Bible.html

---

## 3. Other views

**Textual notes (netbible.org):** the Hebrew of v. 36 needs clarifying from Genesis 36:12, and "Zephi/Zepho" varies between manuscripts. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=1Ch&chapter=1

**Older critical debate (as reported by Keil & Delitzsch, Lutheran):** they argue against Bertheau's attempt to count 70 tribes in vv. 28–42. They point out that the text gives only 69, and that he had to make Timna a grandchild to get there. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/1-38.htm

**Catholic, Orthodox, and popular modern teaching:** nothing found.
